posts.title: Organizations invest heavily in protecting their critical systems.
posts.author: Evolution Technology Group
posts.snippet:
Organizations invest heavily in protecting their critical systems.
Far fewer examine the technology trusted beneath them.

On August 12, a hacker known as ZeroBytes claimed to have accessed the French tax administration’s internal systems and extracted a partial dataset of 678,438 taxpayer and business records. The leak was confirmed by the DGFiP and made public the following day. The exposed records contain full legal names, dates and places of birth, addresses, marital status, number of dependents, tax identification numbers, reference taxable income, withholding tax rates, phone numbers, email addresses, and correspondence logs.

What's most concerning isn't the headline.
It's where the weakness existed.
Not in the network.
Not in the exchange.
Not in the blockchain.
Inside the firmware trusted to protect the asset.
This highlights an important shift in the threat landscape.
The incident underscores the risk that personal data leaks pose to crypto users in jurisdictions with a high prevalence of such attacks.

Organizations must now treat firmware and trusted software as part of their security perimeter or risk model.
• Apply verified firmware updates promptly.
• Strengthen passphrase protection for critical assets.
• Validate key-generation processes across all platforms.
• Monitor vendor security advisories closely.
• Review digital-asset custody controls rigorously.

Attackers increasingly target overlooked infrastructure, trusted software, developer tools, supply chains, devices, dependencies or operational workflows. This trend directly impacts the security of personal data and financial assets, especially in jurisdictions with a high risk of physical extortion tactics like wrench attacks.

The question organizations should be asking is:
How confident are you that your organization's firmware and trusted software are secure?

Read more: https://lnkd.in/dskCCpKS
#DataLeak #Cybersecurity #BlockchainSecurity #FirmwareSecurity #DigitalIdentity #RegulationAndCompliance #ETG #EvolutionTechnologyGroup #dAppLab
posts.reason: Firmware and supply-chain vulnerability discussion directly appeals to CISOs, IT directors and DPOs in scope for NIS2/DORA compliance.

comments.text: Worth separating two risk vectors here: firmware/supply-chain compromise creates the data leak, but it's the correlation of that leaked personal data with on-chain holdings that turns it into a physical extortion risk - the two need different mitigations.
Has anyone seen firmware-level attestation actually adopted as a standard control for custody providers, or is this still mostly a paper requirement in risk frameworks?

In our casework, the data leak itself is rarely the endpoint - it's the second-order use, doxxing wallet holders for wrench attacks, that drives urgency, so timelines for notification and address-hygiene advice matter as much as the technical patch.

posts.author: Damilola Ademodi

Last week in crypto: three stories that tell you where institutional trust is actually going

A breach at Trezor’s shipping partner exposed the home addresses of 14,000 hardware wallet owners this week. 

Devices and keys were never touched, the exposure came through a third-party analytics vulnerability at the shipping provider, not Trezor itself. 

But the 2020 precedent at Ledger is the reason this matters beyond phishing risk: a verified list of “who owns a hardware wallet and where they live” led to real extortion attempts, not just spam emails.

Meanwhile, two stories moved in opposite directions on institutional trust. 

Binance began cutting ties with HTX and 15 other platforms this week, driven by EU, UK, and US sanctions tied to Russia and Iran, upstream compliance enforcement rather than sanctions bodies chasing individual violators after the fact.

And Goldman Sachs agreed to acquire NEOS Investments for up to $2.25 billion, instantly becoming a top-eight active ETF manager with Bitcoin and Ethereum income funds in its portfolio. 

That’s TradFi buying its way into crypto-native yield products rather than building them from scratch.

Full breakdown in the comments.

comments.text: The Ledger precedent is the right comparison, but it's worth noting the mechanism: it wasn't the leaked list itself that enabled extortion, it was combining it with on-chain balance verification - which is exactly why address reuse and public wallet disclosure remain underrated risks for holders.

Forensic Audit in Bangladesh’s Banking Sector: Beyond Finding Irregularities

A conventional audit may identify whether transactions and financial statements comply with applicable requirements.
But forensic audit asks deeper questions:
What happened? How did it happen? Where did the money go? Who was involved? And what evidence supports the findings?

🏦 A Bangladesh Banking Example
Consider a hypothetical situation involving a corporate loan in a Bangladeshi bank.

A borrower receives a substantial credit facility after submitting financial statements, collateral documents and other supporting information.
Later, the account starts showing repayment problems.

A conventional audit may identify:
🔹 Documentation deficiencies
🔹 Exceptions in the credit approval process

But a forensic audit can go further.
It may examine:
🔎 Whether the borrower's financial statements were artificially strengthened before obtaining the facility
🔎 Whether collateral valuation was reasonable and properly supported
🔎 Whether the same assets were used as security for multiple facilities
🔎 Whether loan proceeds were transferred to related or connected businesses

The investigation can then reconstruct the fund-flow trail:
Loan Disbursement → Borrower’s Account → Subsequent Transfers → Connected/Related Accounts → Ultimate Beneficiary

This approach can help the bank understand not merely that a loan became problematic, but whether there were underlying financial or control issues that contributed to the loss.
Forensic audit can complement these frameworks by providing a more investigative approach when there are red flags, suspected fraud, unusual transactions or significant control failures.

🔍 Areas Where Forensic Audit Can Add Value
For Bangladeshi banks, forensic techniques can be particularly useful in:
✅ Loan and advance investigations
✅ Fund diversion and tracing
✅ Suspicious transaction analysis
✅ Related-party and connected lending reviews

💡 The Key Difference

Traditional Audit:
“Are the financial records and controls compliant and fairly presented?”
Forensic Audit:
“What actually happened, how did it happen, what was the financial impact, and what evidence can establish the facts?”
Forensic audit should therefore not be viewed only as a post-fraud exercise.
It can also be a powerful tool for risk identification, control improvement and protection of depositors’ and shareholders’ interests.

Private investigation looks a little different than most people imagine.

Surveillance and field work can absolutely be part of an investigation, but much of the work happens long before anyone ever picks up a camera.

A strong investigation often means sorting through public records, identifying and verifying individuals, tracing family and professional connections, reviewing court and property records, researching assets, analyzing social media and other online information, making calls, and comparing information across multiple sources.

And finding information is only part of the job.

The real value is knowing which information matters, how the pieces connect, and when something doesn’t add up.

A name appearing in a database doesn’t automatically make it the right person. An address doesn’t necessarily mean someone still lives there. An obituary, social media profile, public record, or online search result can provide an important lead, but each source is only one piece of a much larger picture.

That’s why our work goes beyond simply running a search. We research, cross-reference, verify, and document our findings so our clients have information they can actually use.

For attorneys, law firms, businesses, and other professionals, sometimes the difference is in what you find.

Other times, it’s in what you know to question.

posts.title: The secondary ASIC market is one of the most inefficient markets in crypto. That inefficiency is an opportunity.
posts.author: Dmitriy S.
posts.snippet:
The secondary ASIC market is one of the most inefficient markets in crypto. That inefficiency is an opportunity.

Used mining hardware trades like used cars -- high information asymmetry, wide bid-ask spreads, and significant quality variation within the same model.

What drives secondhand ASIC pricing:

- Hashprice: When hashprice is high, used machines get bid up because buyers want immediate deployment. When hashprice compresses, used hardware drops 40-60% in weeks.
- New model announcements: The day Bitmain announces S25 specs, every S21 in the secondary market loses 15-20% of its value overnight.
- Bulk discount curves: A single S21 sells for $3,500-4,000 retail. A pallet of 100 sells for $2,800-3,200 per unit. The discount for quantity is real and consistent.
- Condition and warranty: Units with remaining manufacturer warranty command 15-25% premium over out-of-warranty hardware. But warranty verification is often unreliable.

The arbitrage opportunities:

- Geographic arbitrage: Miners shutting down in high-power-cost regions sell at distressed prices. Those same machines deployed at $0.055/kWh are immediately profitable.
- Cycle arbitrage: Buying used hardware 3-4 months after a halving -- when overleveraged operators are liquidating -- and deploying into the subsequent recovery.
- Efficiency-class arbitrage: Sometimes a slightly older, less efficient machine at 60% of the price per TH delivers better ROI than cutting-edge hardware at full retail.

Risks to manage:

- Hash board condition is invisible until you power on. Budget 5-10% of used fleet purchases for DOA units.
- Firmware locks on some manufacturers' machines restrict third-party deployment.
- Stolen hardware exists in the secondary market. Verify serial numbers against manufacturer databases.

At Rax Mining, we help hosted clients evaluate secondary market purchases as part of fleet planning. Sometimes the right machine isn't the newest one.

What's the oldest ASIC generation you'd still consider deploying at today's hashprice?

posts.title: A hardware wallet can remain secure while its owner becomes the target.
posts.author: ROHIT JR
posts.snippet:
A hardware wallet can remain secure while its owner becomes the target.
As a second-year cybersecurity student, I assumed a hardware-wallet breach would only be serious if private keys or recovery phrases were stolen. SafePal’s latest disclosure changed my perspective.
On August 16, 2026, SafePal disclosed that an authorization flaw in an order-tracking plug-in exposed information belonging to approximately 39,798 customers who placed orders between March 2, 2025 and April 11, 2026.
The exposed information included:
🔹 Names
🔹 Email addresses
🔹 Phone numbers
🔹 Shipping addresses
🔹 Purchase details
SafePal said seed phrases, private keys, wallet passwords, payment-card details and customer funds were not compromised.
But does that make the exposed information low risk?
An attacker who knows someone’s name, address and exact hardware-wallet purchase can create a convincing phishing message:
“Your device has a security problem. Enter your recovery phrase to receive a replacement.”
The leaked information could also reveal where a person believed to own cryptocurrency lives, creating both digital and possible physical-security risks.
The lesson I learned is that securing the main product is not enough. A strong hardware wallet can still be surrounded by vulnerable systems such as:
➡️ E-commerce platforms
➡️ Order-tracking plug-ins
➡️ Customer-support systems
➡️ Logistics providers
➡️ Stored shipping records
One weak authorization control in a supporting service can reduce the security of the entire customer journey.
SafePal says it fixed the flaw, introduced additional protections and notified affected customers. Reports also claim that the stolen information is being offered for sale, although I could not independently confirm that claim.
I would genuinely value the views of AppSec, SOC and crypto-security professionals:
Should the identity and shipping information of hardware-wallet buyers be classified almost as sensitively as authentication data?
What monitoring could detect systematic access to other customers’ orders through a tracking system?
How should companies balance legal data-retention requirements against the security benefits of deleting customer information?
This incident reminded me that breach impact should be measured by what an attacker can do with exposed data—not only by whether passwords or private keys were stolen.

I think I’ve been guilty of hearing “crypto crime” and immediately thinking: this must be incredibly complicated.
Turns out, not necessarily!
Last night was my first CryptoMondays London event, attending a really interesting discussion on crypto crime, illicit funds and asset recovery. In short, take away the crypto buzzwords and a lot of what we’re dealing with is familiar financial crime, just with a new layer of technology.
Erica Stanford spoke about pig butchering and the amount of social engineering behind these crimes, such as grooming victims, building trust and eventually directing them towards spoof websites. The technology may be different, but the human behaviour behind the crime really isn’t.
Charlotte Miller Int.Dip (AML) put it perfectly; to paraphrase, fraud is still fraud and money laundering is still money laundering. Add wallets, blockchains and crypto into the conversation and suddenly it sounds far more mysterious than it necessarily is.

ASIC has issued several scam warnings in quick succession.
And the methods are getting harder to recognise at a glance.

In recent months, ASIC has warned about criminals:
• copying the names, licence numbers and websites of financial services businesses
• using fake celebrity endorsements in investment scams
• creating AI-generated deepfakes, fake news articles, reviews and investment platforms
• impersonating ASIC staff through targeted spear-phishing emails

One recent example shows how convincing this can get.

Scammers used real footage of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, altered with fake audio, to promote a supposed investment opportunity and promise extraordinary returns.

Anthony Albanese was the most impersonated public figure identified by ASIC in FY26. Scamwatch reports show $7.4 million in losses involving the 10 most impersonated public figures.

And this is happening at scale.

ASIC removed more than 19,400 online scams last financial year, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 3,106 #crypto investment scams.

For reporting entities, there are a few things worth thinking about.

A customer caught in a #scam may suddenly start sending money in ways that don’t fit their usual activity.

They may be following instructions from someone they believe is legitimate.

They may send funds to unfamiliar third parties, investment platforms or crypto wallets.

Your own business and staff may also be targeted through impersonation, phishing or spoofed communications.

So it is worth checking:
• whether customer monitoring can identify meaningful changes in transaction behaviour
• whether staff recognise possible scam indicators
• whether unusual activity is reviewed in the context of what you know about the customer
• whether staff know when and how to escalate concerns
• whether unusual communications are independently verified
• whether your SMR process covers situations where a customer may be the victim of a crime

Unusual activity does not automatically mean an #SMR is required.
But when the information gives rise to reasonable grounds for suspicion, the reporting obligation needs to be considered.

Scam methods are changing quickly. Reporting entities need to make sure their monitoring and escalation processes are keeping up.

Talk to us if you need help reviewing or updating your AML/CTF Program, ML/TF Risk Assessment, customer monitoring, scam red flags and suspicious matter escalation procedures.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams in the past year — up 182%. That number should stop you mid-scroll.

Criminal networks are now building entire fake ecosystems using AI deepfakes of trusted figures like Alan Kohler and Anthony Albanese to push fraudulent investment schemes. (ABC News)

But here is the question nobody in our industry is asking:

If AI can generate a convincing video of a public figure endorsing a scam, what happens when that same technology is used to fabricate photographic evidence in an active investigation?

We talk about deepfakes as a consumer fraud problem. A$7.4 million in reported losses this financial year alone. That is real. But for investigators, the threat is different. The photos and videos you collect as evidence now exist in a world where any image can be synthetically generated or altered.

Manual visual comparison was already unreliable. Now it is actively dangerous. Your eyes cannot catch what algorithms can measure. Euclidean distance analysis does not get fooled by a well-crafted composite. Your gut feeling does.

The same technology that creates the problem — AI — is the only thing that can reliably detect it at scale. Investigators who are still comparing faces by eye are not just slow. They are exposed.

When fabricated evidence becomes this easy to produce, how do you prove your real evidence is real?

posts.title: @Athanasius Tesfaye(Athni)
posts.author: John Daniel
posts.snippet:
@Athanasius Tesfaye(Athni)
I never imagined I would end up telling a story like this.

A few months earlier, I had met a man named Athanasius Tesfaye. Everyone called him Athni.

He introduced himself as the CEO of a growing international company—an ambitious man who claimed he was building something that would change the future.

And he was convincing.

Athni didn't speak like an ordinary businessman. He spoke about purpose. Leadership. Sacrifice. Dreams.

Every conversation with him felt like a motivational speech. He talked about entrepreneurs who had started with nothing, fought through impossible odds, and eventually changed the world.

He told us he wasn't simply building a company.

He was building a movement.

And I believed him.

When he offered me a job, I felt fortunate. He told me my skills mattered. He said he saw potential in me.

For someone trying to build a career, hearing that can mean everything.

The salary wasn't extraordinary, but the opportunity seemed enormous. He promised growth, investment, and expansion into international markets.

We were told to work hard. To think bigger. To believe that success was just ahead of us.

So that's what I did.

I worked.

Days became weeks.

Weeks became months.

Then payday came.

And that's when everything changed.

At first, Athni said there were delays with international transfers.

Then there were problems with banking regulations.

After that, he blamed U.S. laws for preventing the payments from going through.

Every week came with a new explanation.

And every explanation came with the same promise:

Soon.

"Just be patient."

"We're almost there."

"Next week. Definitely."

We heard those words so many times that they became part of the routine.

Some employees began asking questions.

Others started getting nervous.

A few simply walked away.

But Athni always had an answer.

And somehow, he always sounded believable.

Looking back, I realize something.

The speeches never stopped.

The promises never stopped.

But the salaries never came.

Eventually, there was nowhere left for the truth to hide.

One day, Athni told us the company was shutting down.

Just like that.

No salaries.
No compensation.
No accountability.

The company that was supposedly going to change the world simply disappeared.

But the money wasn't the part that hurt the most.

It was realizing that the vision had been a tool.

The inspiration had been a tool.

The promises had been a tool.

We thought we were employees working toward a dream.

In reality, our trust had been exploited.

For months, I blamed myself for believing him.

But I've learned something since then.

Scams don't always look like scams.

Sometimes they look like opportunity.

Sometimes they sound like inspiration.

The lesson is simple.

Don't judge a company by what it promises.

Judge it by what it does.

A real company pays its employees.
And a real vision doesn't disappear the moment it's time to take responsibility.

posts.title: A suspected affiliate of The Gentlemen ransomware operation used Anthropic's Claude Code to carry out hands-on cyber intrusions across at least eight global organizations, automati
posts.author: Jan Sobczyk
posts.snippet:
A suspected affiliate of The Gentlemen ransomware operation used Anthropic's Claude Code to carry out hands-on cyber intrusions across at least eight global organizations, automating steps from initial VPN exploitation to data exfiltration. 

AI is no longer just assisting attackers with writing phishing emails; it is now executing live exploitation, credential theft, and data exfiltration with minimal human oversight: 

"The most striking technique involved a classic LDAP pass-back attack executed almost entirely by AI. Claude edited a FortiGate firewall’s VPN authentication settings so it would validate logins against the attacker’s own machine instead of the victim’s domain controllers, then wrote a Python LDAP listener on the fly and deployed it on port 389. After several attempts, a '"diagnose test authserver"' command tricked the firewall into sending its service account password in cleartext to the rogue listener, after which Claude restored the original configuration to avoid detection.
Claude’s own log candidly admitted the mistake: '"Yeah, I screwed up – I shouldn’t have done a full config restore."' External scans confirmed the appliance remained unreachable afterward."

#CyberSecurity #ArtificialIntelligence #Ransomware #InfoSec #AICyberSecurity #Claude #CyberThreats #NetworkSecurity

Se um arquivo importante for apagado do seu Microsoft 365 hoje, quem garante que ele volta?

A resposta surpreende muita gente: a Microsoft garante que o serviço esteja no ar, não que os seus dados sejam recuperados. Isso é o modelo de responsabilidade compartilhada a infraestrutura é dela, os dados são seus.

Uma política de backup dedicada para o Microsoft 365 resolve isso: retenção definida pela sua empresa, restauração ponto a ponto e cobertura de e-mail, Teams, SharePoint e OneDrive.

Fale com a BRLIC e entenda como proteger o que está no seu 365.

posts.title: 𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗗 (𝗥𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗿𝗿𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀) 💾
posts.author: Daniyal Z.
posts.snippet:
𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗗 (𝗥𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗿𝗿𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀) 💾

You might have heard this term already. Let’s take a deeper look.

RAID combines multiple physical disks into one logical storage unit to improve:
↳ Performance
↳ Availability
↳ Fault Tolerance
↳ Capacity

There are 𝟯 main concepts behind RAID:

⚡ 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 — Distributing data across multiple disks to improve performance.

⧉ 𝗠𝗶𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 — Storing the same data on multiple disks for redundancy.

🧮 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 — Storing calculated information that can reconstruct missing data without keeping a full duplicate.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸? 🧮
Parity can be calculated using XOR.
A ⊕ B = P
So if B is lost, it can be reconstructed:
A ⊕ P = B

And yes, even within RAID, 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙚𝙨 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝 𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙙𝙚-𝙤𝙛𝙛𝙨.

𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗗 𝟬 – 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴

RAID 0 provides 𝗭𝗘𝗥𝗢 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗰𝘆.

Suppose a file contains:
A B C D E F
Disk 1 → A C E
Disk 2 → B D F
Both disks can work in parallel, improving throughput and aggregate disk bandwidth.

⚖️ 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲-𝗼𝗳𝗳: If either disk fails, the array becomes unusable.

𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗗 𝟭 – 𝗠𝗶𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴

RAID 1 stores the same data on multiple disks.

Disk 1 → A B C D
Disk 2 → A B C D
If one disk fails, the other still contains the data. Reads may also be served from either disk.

⚖️ 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲-𝗼𝗳𝗳: You sacrifice storage efficiency. Significant cost of doubling your disks.

𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗗 𝟱 – 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 + 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆

RAID 5 combines striping with 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 and requires at least 3 disks.

Disk 1 | Disk 2 | Disk 3
A | B | P1
C | P2 | D
P3 | E | F
If 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀, its data can be reconstructed using the remaining data and parity.

⚖️ 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲-𝗼𝗳𝗳: Parity adds write overhead, and RAID 5 tolerates only 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲.

𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗗 𝟲 – 𝗗𝗼𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆

RAID 6 uses two independent parity values, allowing the array to survive 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀.

⚖️ 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲-𝗼𝗳𝗳: More fault tolerance, but less usable capacity and additional write overhead.

IMPORTANT: 𝙍𝘼𝙄𝘿 𝙞𝙨 𝙉𝙊𝙏 𝙖 𝙗𝙖𝙘𝙠𝙪𝙥.

RAID protects against disk failures, but not necessarily against:
↳ Accidental deletion
↳ Corrupted writes
↳ Ransomware
↳ Server or datacenter failure

That’s why production systems may combine:

𝙍𝘼𝙄𝘿 + 𝙍𝙚𝙥𝙡𝙞𝙘𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 + 𝘽𝙖𝙘𝙠𝙪𝙥𝙨 + 𝘿𝙞𝙨𝙖𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙍𝙚𝙘𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮

Each solves a different failure scenario.

There’s still much more to RAID: rebuilds, hot spares, RAID 10/50/60, write penalties, hardware vs software RAID, and write holes.
All RAID concepts might not fit into LinkedIn posts, so I might write a detailed article on this one.

𝙎𝙩𝙖𝙮 𝙩𝙪𝙣𝙚𝙙! 👀

♻️ Repost if you find this helpful.

posts.author: CMIT OCALA
posts.snippet:
Regaining Trust After Breach(s)

🚨 When Government Gets Hacked, It's Not Just Data at Risk — It's Trust.
A large county in Florida recently fell victim to a malware attack. While the full scope of damage is still being assessed, one thing is already clear: the real casualty isn't just systems or data — it's the confidence taxpayers place in their government.
Think about that for a moment. Residents pay their taxes expecting roads to be maintained, permits to be processed, emergency services to be funded — and yes, their personal information to be protected. When a cyberattack disrupts that, the silent question every taxpayer asks is:
"Were you ready? And what are you doing about it?"
Silence is not an answer.
🔍 Here's what responsible government looks like after an incident:
✅ A public-facing After Action Report (AAR) — not a watered-down press release, but a genuine account of what happened, what failed, and what's being fixed.
✅ A technical review conducted or validated by an independent third party — not just internal IT teams evaluating their own work.
✅ Transparency about taxpayer impact — what data was exposed, what systems were offline, and what it cost to remediate.
✅ A roadmap for improvement — with timelines and accountability baked in.
This isn't about blame. Sophisticated threat actors target governments every single day. No organization is immune. But the difference between a government that erodes public trust and one that strengthens it comes down to one thing: accountability in the aftermath.
Taxpayers don't expect perfection. They expect honesty and action.
If your county, city, or agency has been hit — the best thing you can do is show your work. Publish the AAR. Hold the briefing. Invite the scrutiny.
Because transparency after a breach isn't weakness. It's leadership.
💬 To cybersecurity professionals, government IT leaders, and policy makers: What does a good public after action process look like to you? I'd love to hear your thoughts below.
#Cybersecurity #PublicSector #GovTech #Ransomware #Malware #Florida #TaxpayerTrust #IncidentResponse #Transparency #CyberResilience #InfoSec
posts.reason: Thoughtful post by government IT leader on accountability after breaches; directly invites discussion from cybersecurity professionals and government officials we target, with clear positioning opportunity.

comments.text: One thing often missing from these AARs: a clear, public distinction between 'we contained it' and 'we know exactly what left the network' — the second requires forensic reconstruction of exfiltration, not just system restoration, and that's the part governments tend to gloss over.

We've seen incident reports where the technical narrative was solid but the taxpayer-facing data impact statement was vague to the point of being useless — the credibility gap usually starts exactly there.

posts.title: This is the part of crypto fraud investigations that I find fascinating.
posts.author: Nicki Sanders
posts.snippet:
This is the part of crypto fraud investigations that I find fascinating.

An arrest tells you who allegedly ran the scheme. It doesn’t tell you where the money went.

$165M came in. Some went to trading losses. Some allegedly went to personal spending. Some was used to pay earlier investors.

But there’s still a massive financial puzzle left to solve:
⭐ How much went to insiders?
⭐ Where did the assets move?
⭐ What was converted to fiat?
⭐ What was transferred through exchanges or other intermediaries?
⭐ What’s still sitting somewhere that can be recovered?

Onchain data gives investigators an incredible starting point, but following the money all the way through requires connecting blockchain activity to bank records, exchange data, investor records, corporate entities, and real-world assets.

That’s where blockchain forensics gets really interesting. The arrest is one milestone, following every dollar is the real investigation.

We've seen the exact pattern you describe — the arrest is treated as the finish line publicly, but internally it's the moment the real tracing work starts, matching wallet clusters against exchange KYC and corporate records to see what's actually recoverable versus just accounted for.

posts.title: ​When NOT to Pay WHT and VAT (Reverse Charge) on a Non-Resident Supplier's Bill?
posts.author: Pedro Maquenha
posts.snippet:
​When NOT to Pay WHT and VAT (Reverse Charge) on a Non-Resident Supplier's Bill?

​The answer might sound obvious, but this is still a major point of doubt for many accountants. Misunderstanding these rules significantly impacts cash flow, even if the funds are theoretically recoverable later.

#VAT Scenarios:

1. ​Chargeability: Ask yourself, if a service provided by a local supplier is exempt from VAT, why should the situation change when it comes to a non-resident service provider? The exemption attaches to the nature of the service or good, not the location of the provider. Therefore, there is no scope for VAT reverse charge.

2. ​Territoriality: Identify where the service is actually performed. If the service is rendered outside the national territory (and falls outside domestic VAT rules for localized services), it is not within Mozambique's tax jurisdiction. Consequently, no VAT reverse charge applies.


#​WHT (Withholding Tax) Scenarios:

1. ​Double Taxation Agreements: Mozambique has bilateral tax treaties with certain countries to prevent double taxation, the income is taxable only in the service provider's country of residence;

2. ​Statutory Exemptions: As a way to encourage specific business activities or sector practices, the government may grant explicit tax exemptions. When an income stream or entity is exempt, withholding tax cannot be deducted;

3. ​Territoriality: If the service is performed entirely outside the national territory, withholding tax does not apply. Generally, only income derived from sources within the national territory is subject to corporate income tax, whether for residents or non-residents.
​
#​Attention:

WHT and VAT are treated separately. The same service may be exempt from VAT but subject to WHT, vice versa, or exempt from both/neither.

​If you think this can help strengthen the accounting community, share it to reach them!

​Finance is not a back office,  finance is a business partner!

​Pedro Maquenha

Why largecaps saw outflows
 
One key reason for profit-booking in largecap funds was recent performance. “Investors rotated towards midcaps and smallcaps, where earnings growth and recent returns have been stronger,” says Bharat Lahoti, president & co-head, factor investing, Edelweiss Mutual Fund.
 
Investors often gravitate towards the segment that has stronger momentum.
Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) sold largely largecap stocks over the previous few quarters, which weighed on sentiment towards this category.

Largecap outlook improving

What drove midcap and smallcap inflows

posts.title: AI concentration risk is moving inside the index fund.
posts.author: Viacheslav Kraft
posts.snippet:
AI concentration risk is moving inside the index fund.

An European Central Bank analysis published on August 17 makes a useful distinction.

The euro area's risk is not limited to investors who directly selected US technology stocks.

Using look-through holdings data, the authors find that most euro-area exposure to the Magnificent Seven sits through mutual funds and ETFs. That places households, insurers and pension funds inside the transmission chain even when their portfolios appear diversified at the product level.

The mechanism is operational:

AI-linked valuations fall → investors redeem fund shares → funds sell liquid assets → price pressure increases → more redemptions become possible.

The European Central Bank authors are not saying AI has no economic value.

Their argument is more uncomfortable: a genuinely transformative technology can still produce an asset-price correction. As adoption spreads, uncertainty that was once company-specific becomes economy-wide. Investors may then require a higher risk premium even if profits continue to grow.

Europe has a partial buffer. Its equity market has lower technology valuations and more “old economy” exposure than the US.

But lower domestic exuberance does not remove imported concentration through global indices or the historically high correlation between US and euro-area markets.

This changes AI risk diligence for asset owners.

A sector-allocation chart is no longer enough. The control ledger should include:

• direct and look-through exposure;
• index concentration and overlapping holdings;
• dependence of earnings on the same AI suppliers and customers;
• fund liquidity and redemption sensitivity;
• collateral and forced-sale requirements;
• governance response time under stress.

This is not a market-timing signal. The ECB analysis does not establish when, how large or whether a correction will occur.

It does show why “we own diversified funds” is not the same as “we have diversified AI risk.”

The next portfolio question is not only how much technology exposure exists.

It is how many different-looking assets depend on the same AI cash-flow story.

Source: European Central Bank Blog, 17 August 2026.

posts.title: Tax-exempt doesn’t mean filing-exempt.
posts.author: Ajjeesh Surenddran
posts.snippet:
Tax-exempt doesn’t mean filing-exempt.
That’s one of the biggest misconceptions I see around nonprofit accounting.
Many nonprofits assume that because they don’t pay federal income tax like a traditional business, their tax deadlines and accounting requirements are less demanding.
They aren’t.
For many tax-exempt organizations:
📌 Form 990/990-EZ is still required annually
📌 The deadline is generally the 15th day of the 5th month after the fiscal year ends
📌 Organizations can generally request a 6-month extension using Form 8868
📌 But an extension gives them more time to file — not permission to stop maintaining their books
And this is where things get interesting.
A nonprofit can have:
• Grants coming from multiple sources
• Restricted vs. unrestricted funds
• Donor contributions
• Program expenses
• Payroll and administrative costs
• Fundraising revenue
• Multiple programs requiring separate tracking
If those transactions aren't properly categorized throughout the year, preparing the 990 becomes much more than a “tax filing” exercise.
It becomes a cleanup exercise.
And that's where good nonprofit bookkeeping matters.
The best approach isn't:
Wait for the 990 deadline → scramble to reconstruct the books → file → repeat next year.
It's:
Monthly bookkeeping → proper fund/restriction tracking → reconciliations → financial reporting → smoother 990 preparation.
For nonprofit leaders, the goal shouldn't simply be to meet the filing deadline.
It should be to have books that are 990-ready throughout the year.
Because being tax-exempt may reduce certain tax obligations.
It doesn't eliminate the need for financial discipline.

posts.title: In July 2007, I walked into UBS for my first day on Wall Street.
posts.author: David Laut

In July 2007, I walked into UBS for my first day on Wall Street.

New suit. Fresh off training in New York. Absolutely convinced I was the man.
That fall, our stock dipped from $90 to $80 after earnings. The employee plan let us buy shares with options attached. And 24-year-old me, living rent-free at my parents' house, saw only one move:

Back up the truck.

I put somewhere between 25% and 50% of my income into UBS stock. I felt like the Wolf of Wall Street.

You know what happened next. The financial crisis hit.
Within a year, UBS went from $80 to $8.

Not down 8%. Eight. Dollars.

That was my tuition payment for a lesson I've now watched play out for two decades — in the mortgage crisis, in the dot-com stories my Intel-retiree clients told me, in crypto, and (I suspect) in what's coming with AI:

The worst money decisions are almost never intelligence failures. They're speed failures.

Somebody feels the wind at their back — a rising stock, a hot sector, easy margin — and they accelerate at exactly the moment they should slow down. Every generation gets its own version. Every generation swears it's different this time.

Buffett said: only when the tide goes out do you discover who's been swimming naked.

Now, when a decision makes me feel euphoric — when I catch myself thinking "this can't lose" — I've learned to treat that feeling as a red light, not a green one.

Slow is not the enemy of wealth. Slow is how wealth survives. God's way. 

New episode titled "The Worst Money Mistakes We've Ever Made" drops today.

🪙 If you've been sitting on the sidelines of crypto because it still feels like the Wild West, this may be one of the more important U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission developments to watch.

And surprisingly, crypto investors may not be the biggest winners.

The SEC is moving toward a clearer regulatory framework for crypto assets, including how certain crypto offerings can operate within U.S. securities laws.

Why does that matter?

Because one of the biggest barriers to broader crypto adoption hasn't just been volatility.

It's been uncertainty.

What is a security?
What isn't?
How can a token legally be issued?
Who can custody it?
How can banks and financial institutions participate?

The clearer those answers become, the easier it becomes for traditional finance to enter the market.

TL;DR

• Investors: Less regulatory ambiguity lowers one barrier to entering crypto. It does NOT eliminate investment risk.

• Crypto companies: Clearer rules could provide a more predictable path for launching products and raising capital in the U.S.

• Banks & financial institutions: Potentially the biggest winners. More clarity can unlock custody, lending, trading, tokenization, and wealth-management products.

• Crypto adoption: The next 100 million users may not enter crypto through a wallet or DeFi protocol. They may encounter it through the financial institutions and products they already use.

That's the part I find most interesting.

We may be watching the progression from:

Alternative financial ecosystem → Regulated asset class → Integrated financial infrastructure

And once that happens, the distinction between "crypto" and "traditional finance" starts becoming less useful.

Your financial life could increasingly look like:

Bank accounts + 401(k) + brokerage + crypto + tokenized assets + real estate + liabilities

The real opportunity may not be another place to buy crypto.

It may be building the intelligence layer that understands all of it together.

That's a big part of the thesis behind Altrion.ai:

Aggregate. Analyze. Advance.

Crypto doesn't need to replace traditional finance to become enormously important.

It just needs to become part of it.

From massive corporate leaks to novel AI threats, the landscape is shifting quickly. Here is a breakdown of the latest incidents and, more importantly, how you can protect yourself.

Hackers exposed over 27 million records via Microsoft Power Pages. Separately, an Azure credential theft impacted major brands like McDonald's, and crypto wallet maker SafePal reported a leak of nearly 40,000 customers' contact and shipping info (though funds remain secure).

Cybercriminals are heavily targeting mobile users with elaborate, highly convincing listings for luxury 5-star hotels that don't exist.

When major breaches hit the news, the fallout always trickles down to regular users. Here is your action plan:

2- Verify Before You Book: Cross-reference travel arrangements on multiple maps and review sites. Always book directly through reputable platforms or official websites.

3- Stay Skeptical of Digital Media: With watermark-removal tools on the rise, don't blindly trust startling images or videos on your feed. Verify through independent sources.

posts.title: This week’s crypto security news is another reminder that we still have some very basic security problems to solve. Privacy gaps and weaknesses in consensus continue to give attack
posts.author: Archimedes Insights
posts.snippet:
This week’s crypto security news is another reminder that we still have some very basic security problems to solve. Privacy gaps and weaknesses in consensus continue to give attackers plenty of opportunities.
We saw a string of PII leaks hit crypto users. Trezor’s shipping partner, ShipMonk, exposed order information for about 14,000 customers, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses. SafePal had a similar incident involving nearly 40,000 orders. Then France’s tax authority confirmed a breach affecting roughly 678,000 people and businesses, including income and withholding information. That raises some obvious concerns about how useful this information could be for targeted attacks.
At the same time, Coldcard users were scrambling to move funds following a major exploit. The bigger issue here is that we still don't do a very good job protecting the information around crypto. Hardware wallet orders, tax records, exchange accounts, and everyday transactions can all give attackers information they can use.
On the blockchain side, Ravencoin had a rare consensus failure where the network accepted blocks without the required ProgPoW work. That has led to plans for a multi-day rollback. Harmony had an even more serious problem. A broken quorum check allowed forged signatures to pass validation, resulting in billions, and later trillions, of ONE tokens being created. A lot of those tokens made their way to exchanges very quickly, and a network rollback is now underway. And if Harmony sounds familiar, its Horizon bridge was also hit for roughly $100 million in 2022 by DPRK-linked attackers.
There was plenty more this week: a Zoom zero-click RCE affecting meeting participants, a White House policy opening the door to private-sector offensive cyber operations against foreign criminals, and Lazarus-linked IT workers exposed through a fake DeFi startup honeypot. There is also new research, better DeFi incident datasets, and new model benchmarks aimed at defenders. The lesson this week is pretty simple: third-party dependencies and basic verification remain weak points. Privacy and solid consensus aren't nice-to-haves in crypto. They are the foundation.
posts.reason: Substantive security incident analysis by a credible voice covering hardware wallet breaches, consensus failures, and exchange risks—exactly the type of post where we could add forensics perspective for compliance and law enforcement audiences.

comments.text: The Harmony rollback detail is worth dwelling on: once forged tokens hit exchanges, the window for a clean choke-point freeze closes fast, which is exactly why speed of exchange notification matters more than sophistication of the exploit itself.

With PII leaks stacking up across hardware wallet vendors and now tax authorities, do you see attackers starting to correlate these datasets to target specific high-balance individuals rather than opportunistic phishing?
We've traced cases where a shipping-partner leak like ShipMonk's became the opening move for a targeted extortion attempt months later — the PII itself is rarely the endgame, it's the reconnaissance.

posts.title: MEXC published its rundown of 2026's ten biggest crypto security incidents this week. The part that matters for marketing, not security, gets buried under the headline number.

MEXC published its rundown of 2026's ten biggest crypto security incidents this week. The part that matters for marketing, not security, gets buried under the headline number.

Everyone already knows the $282 million figure: a hardware wallet user talked into approving his own transfer, no code touched. The list around it is the part worth reading slowly. Legacy contracts still getting exploited years after ship date. Frameworks inherited as dependencies, carrying risk no one on the current team reviewed. A technical standard the industry adopted before anyone stress-tested it in production.

None of those four incidents share a root cause. What they share is where the audit stops looking. A code review covers the repo a team wrote. It says nothing about the support script a rep followed, the framework a contractor pulled in two years ago, or the standard nobody questioned at launch.

For agencies pitching a client's security posture, that gap sits directly under the brand promise. A disclosure does not wait to check whether the flaw was in the client's own code before it costs them trust. Community management and onboarding flows need a security-education layer built in now, not added after an incident report. And as AI agents start executing on-chain actions on a client's behalf, they carry the same exposure a support rep does: a request they can be talked into approving.

posts.title: Legacy code and inherited dependencies show up in more of 2026's biggest crypto security incidents than fresh smart contract bugs do.
posts.author: James Williams
posts.snippet:
Legacy code and inherited dependencies show up in more of 2026's biggest crypto security incidents than fresh smart contract bugs do.

MEXC's rundown of this year's ten largest losses makes the pattern easy to see in one list. A hardware wallet holder talked into approving his own $282 million transfer. Contracts written years ago, still running, still unreviewed. Frameworks pulled in as dependencies, carrying risk nobody on the current team ever checked. A technical standard the industry shipped before anyone stress-tested it under real conditions.

None of those four incidents trace back to a fresh bug in this year's code. Each one came from something a team stopped looking at once the initial audit passed.

Teams doing security due diligence on a client's stack tend to ask one question: has this been audited. The list above shows that question stops too early. Inherited dependencies and legacy contracts don't fall inside a launch-day audit scope, because they predate the audit.

The more useful due-diligence question for agencies vetting a Web3 client is narrower than "has this been audited." It's what in this stack is older than the current team, and whether anyone is still watching it.

posts.reason: Solid analysis of inherited risk and legacy systems in Web3 security that would interest due-diligence teams, but primarily advisory rather than invoking our forensics or recovery capabilities.

comments.text: That $282M case is also a useful reminder that once funds move, the forensic clock starts immediately - the window for effective choke-point analysis at centralised exchanges narrows fast once the money starts hopping bridges and mixers. Legacy code gets the headlines, but the post-incident tracing outcome is often decided in the first 24-48 hours, not by how the breach happened.
Do you see teams building any kind of continuous dependency and contract monitoring after audit sign-off, or is 'audited once' still treated as a permanent status by most Web3 orgs you look at?

We see the mirror image of this in tracing work: victims and their advisors often focus entirely on how the breach happened, when the more urgent question is where the funds went and how fast. The root-cause question matters for prevention, but it rarely helps the tracing timeline.
